input_signals.name: PreDepreciationAccrualsVsEquityDepletion
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ib, oancf), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Stripping depreciation out of total accruals isolates the discretionary, reversible component, and this component is most damaging for firms with depleted or negative retained earnings, which have exhausted their internally generated equity cushion and face the strongest incentive to manage reported earnings.
input_signals.reasoning: Depreciation is a mechanical, non-discretionary accrual that dilutes the earnings-management content of total accruals, so adding it back sharpens the accrual leg. Retained-earnings deficit measures chronic cumulative failure rather than a capital-structure choice, so it is a distress channel distinct from leverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( sub( ib, oancf ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SloanAccrualsWeakCashCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: High balance-sheet accruals are most damaging for firms whose cash earnings barely cover total liabilities, because such firms cannot absorb the reversal and must fund it with external capital raised on punitive terms.
input_signals.reasoning: This unites the two channels that carried signal in generation 1 (accruals net of depreciation, and cash-earnings debt coverage) while replacing the coverage-destroying cash-flow-statement items with balance-sheet deltas, which should roughly double or triple usable observations and stabilize the long-short legs. If both the FMB t-stat and the alpha t-stat strengthen relative to AccrualBuildupVsCashDebtCoverage, the earlier weakness was a data-availability artifact rather than a mechanism failure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SignedSloanAccrualsLeverageWeighted
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), at), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Leverage amplifies the price impact of accruals symmetrically: for a debt-heavy firm, positive accruals signal an imminent earnings reversal it cannot finance, while negative accruals signal genuine cash generation and deleveraging capacity that the market underappreciates.
input_signals.reasoning: Holding the accrual construction identical to Signal 1, this isolates one design choice—preserving the signed magnitude of accruals and using leverage only as a non-negative amplification weight, versus double-ranking both legs. Comparing the two tells us whether the accrual tail magnitude or merely its cross-sectional rank carries the interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( mul( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AccrualsPerUnitEquityCushion
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), ceq), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is the size of the accrual relative to the loss-absorbing equity base, not relative to assets: a given dollar of soft earnings threatens solvency far more when book equity is thin, so accruals per unit of equity cushion is itself an accrual-distress interaction.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the asset denominator with book equity embeds the distress conditioning directly into the scaling rather than through a separate multiplicative leg, which avoids the noise of estimating two ranks and mechanically overweights thinly capitalized firms. Winsorization controls the explosive tail when equity approaches zero.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), ceq ), 1 )

input_signals.name: SloanAccrualsTwoChannelFragility
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt)), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial fragility has a flow dimension (cash earnings cannot cover liabilities) and a stock dimension (the retained-earnings base is depleted); accrual reversals are most punishing where both hold, because the firm has neither current cash flow nor accumulated equity to absorb them.
input_signals.reasoning: The two distress proxies that carried signal separately in generations 1 and 2 — cash-earnings coverage and retained-earnings deficit — are combined into one rank-summed fragility score before interacting with the best-performing accrual leg. Averaging two noisy fragility measures should reduce classification error at the distress margin, which is where the long-short portfolio composition was previously unstable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), rank( sumrank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryNeutralAccrualCoverageInteraction
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Both accrual intensity and debt-coverage capacity are strongly industry-determined (utilities and retailers are structurally levered and inventory-heavy), so the economically meaningful interaction is between a firm's accrual aggressiveness and its fragility *relative to industry peers*, not in absolute terms.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates exactly one design choice against the generation-2 flagship — industry-relative versus pooled ranking — so the comparison is diagnostic rather than cosmetic. If the alpha and FMB t-stat both improve, a large part of the residual noise in the long-short spread is sector tilt rather than mispricing, which would direct all remaining refinements toward industry-neutral construction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationSuppressionVsCashCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, at), 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Suppressing depreciation is an earnings-management lever pulled hardest by firms whose cash flow cannot service debt, because a non-cash charge can be stretched without any cash consequence while preserving reported coverage ratios for lenders.
input_signals.reasoning: Holding the depreciation-policy accrual leg fixed and swapping stock leverage for flow-based coverage tests whether the archive's largest alpha (−4.5%, t = −3.88) is driven by debt *load* or by debt-service *capacity*, which are economically different mechanisms. Cash coverage was the distress leg that worked best with working-capital accruals, so if it also dominates here the two accrual channels share a single conditioning variable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( delta( ratio( dp, at ), 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DualAccrualChannelVsCashCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, at), 1)), RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, ADD(dlc, txp)), 1)), dp), at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms manage earnings on two margins simultaneously — inflating working-capital accruals and suppressing depreciation — and a firm doing both while unable to cover its liabilities from cash earnings is the purest case of unsustainable reported profit.
input_signals.reasoning: The two accrual legs that each worked with cash coverage are economically complementary (current versus non-current accruals) and their errors should be largely independent, so rank-summing them before the distress interaction should raise the signal-to-noise of the accrual dimension. This is a consolidation of the two best archive channels rather than a new mechanism, and it directly tests whether they are additive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sumrank( neg( delta( ratio( dp, at ), 1 ) ), ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, add( dlc, txp ) ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryNeutralDepreciationCoverageInteraction
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, at), 1))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Depreciation rates and debt-coverage capacity are heavily determined by asset intensity and industry norms, so a firm's depreciation suppression and fragility are only informative relative to peers facing the same accounting conventions and capital structure norms.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry-relative ranking improved the alpha and Sharpe of the Sloan-accrual interaction in generation 3, and the depreciation channel should benefit even more because depreciation-to-assets is almost mechanically an industry characteristic. This isolates one design choice against the current leader, so the comparison is diagnostic.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( delta( ratio( dp, at ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationBelowOwnNormVsCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A one-year fall in the depreciation rate can be ordinary asset-mix churn, whereas a depreciation rate sitting below the firm's own three-year norm indicates a deliberate, sustained stretching of asset lives that must eventually reverse through impairment.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the first difference with a deviation from the firm's own recent average filters transitory noise while keeping the same economic content, which should improve slope precision without the directional-extrapolation failure that sank the generation-1 trend signal. If both statistics improve over the leader, the mechanism is a persistent policy state rather than a one-year event.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 3 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationShortfallVsBlendedFragility
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(che, ceq), lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragility that makes depreciation suppression dangerous has a flow component (cash earnings cannot service liabilities) and a stock component (little cash or equity to absorb a write-down), and firms scoring badly on both are the ones whose stretched asset lives will be forcibly corrected.
input_signals.reasoning: The generation-4 diagnostic showed the two distress legs carry complementary evidence — coverage produces the FMB slope, balance-sheet solvency produces the larger and more reliable alpha — so rank-summing them before the interaction should retain both forms of evidence rather than trading one for the other. This is the most direct consolidation of the archive's strongest result.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 3 ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ), neg( ratio( add( che, ceq ), lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationShortfallLongMemory
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset-life stretching is a slow policy drift rather than a one-year event, so measuring the depreciation rate against a five-year norm should capture more of the cumulative deferred expense than a three-year benchmark.
input_signals.reasoning: Moving from a one-year difference to a three-year norm raised the FMB t-stat from −2.98 to −3.73 and the Sharpe from −0.26 to −0.40, so the horizon of the benchmark is clearly a live design parameter worth one more step. The cost is a longer history requirement, so coverage relative to 0.141 is the key diagnostic for whether the gain is real or a survivorship artifact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeerRelativeDepreciationShortfallVsCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Depreciation policy is governed by industry asset composition, so a firm's shortfall is only evidence of manipulation when it is unusual relative to peers experiencing the same asset-mix shifts; fragility, by contrast, is comparable economy-wide.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry-neutralizing both legs previously helped the working-capital interaction's alpha but slightly hurt the depreciation version's FMB slope, suggesting the sector information in the *distress* leg is genuine while that in the accrual leg is noise. Applying IND_RANK asymmetrically tests exactly that asymmetry, which no prior signal has done.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 3 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: OperatingAssetGrowthOutrunningDepreciation
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(at, che), 1), GROWTH(dp, 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's operating asset base grows materially faster than its depreciation charge, capitalized costs are accumulating on the balance sheet without a matching expense, and for a firm that cannot cover its liabilities from cash earnings those capitalized costs are impairment candidates rather than productive assets.
input_signals.reasoning: This reframes the depreciation channel as a matching failure between the asset base and its expense rather than as a deviation from the firm's own rate, which is a different economic statement and a different statistic. The generation-3 sales-benchmarked version lost its slope, but sales is a demand variable whereas operating assets are the actual depreciable base, so this is the economically correct benchmark for the same idea.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( sub( at, che ), 1 ), growth( dp, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationShortfallVsInterestBearingCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Hard default risk comes from contractual debt with fixed maturities and covenants, not from payables and deferred items, so cash-earnings coverage of interest-bearing debt should identify the firms whose accounting choices are driven by financing constraints more precisely than coverage of total liabilities.
input_signals.reasoning: Total liabilities mixes trade credit and operating provisions with contractual borrowing, which blurs the incentive story that motivates the whole design; narrowing the denominator to `dltt + dlc` is a single, well-motivated change to the leading signal's distress leg. If the slope and alpha both improve, the mechanism is specifically covenant and refinancing pressure rather than general liability weight.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 3 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: StandardizedDepreciationShortfallVsCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), VOL(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A given drop in the depreciation rate is meaningful evidence of manipulation only for firms whose depreciation rate is normally stable; for firms with naturally volatile asset mixes the same drop is noise, so the shortfall should be measured in units of the firm's own historical volatility.
input_signals.reasoning: Scaling the shortfall by its firm-specific standard deviation converts a raw deviation into a surprise measure, which should concentrate the short leg on genuine accounting decisions rather than on capital-intensity churn and thereby raise both the slope precision and the Sharpe ratio. This is the natural statistical sharpening of the leading signal and it also tests whether the second-moment information that failed as a standalone accrual-instability signal becomes useful as a normalizer.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 3 ) ), vol( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: LongMemoryDepreciationShortfallVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose depreciation rate has drifted persistently below their own five-year norm while cash earnings barely cover contractual debt are stretching asset lives to preserve covenant headroom, and the deferred expense is later forced out through impairments.
input_signals.reasoning: This joins the two independently validated improvements from generation 5 — the five-year norm (best FMB slope) and the interest-bearing debt denominator (best alpha and Sharpe) — which were each tested against the same baseline and should be close to orthogonal design choices. If both statistics improve simultaneously it establishes the consolidated specification for the remaining generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeerRelativeLongMemoryShortfallVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Depreciation shortfalls are most diagnostic when they are unusual relative to industry peers experiencing the same asset-mix and technology shifts, while debt-service capacity remains comparable across the whole market.
input_signals.reasoning: Asymmetric industry-neutralization of only the accrual leg modestly improved the slope at the three-year horizon, so it is worth one test on top of the consolidated specification to see whether the sector component of a five-year drift is noise or signal. Pairing it with Signal 1 isolates exactly one design choice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationBelowOwnPeakVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cumulative amount of deferred depreciation expense is best measured against the highest rate the firm ever charged on a comparable asset base, since that peak reveals the depreciation intensity the assets genuinely require; the gap below the peak is the accumulated unrecognized charge.
input_signals.reasoning: A mean benchmark is contaminated by the firm's own recent suppression, mechanically shrinking the measured shortfall for serial manipulators, whereas a five-year maximum anchors on the firm's least-managed year and is monotone in cumulative stretching. This is a genuinely different statistic of the same economic state, not a window tweak, and it should sharpen the short leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ts_max( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationShortfallVsDebtFlowAndStock
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc))), RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Refinancing pressure has a flow dimension (cash earnings relative to debt) and a stock dimension (net interest-bearing debt relative to assets), and combining them within the debt family identifies constrained firms more accurately than either alone.
input_signals.reasoning: The earlier blend failed because it mixed in cash-plus-equity solvency, a skewed stock measure that destroyed the linear slope; net debt to assets is smoothly distributed and belongs to the same contractual-obligation channel that just proved dominant. This tests whether blending helps when both components come from the correct economic family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ), ratio( sub( add( dltt, dlc ), che ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationShortfallAtMaturityWall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The incentive to flatter reported earnings peaks when debt must be rolled imminently, so the share of borrowing that is current — a maturity wall — identifies the firms for which accounting choices are most consequential, independently of how profitable or levered they are.
input_signals.reasoning: Every distress leg tested so far measures the size or serviceability of debt, never its timing, yet refinancing risk is fundamentally a maturity-structure concept and is nearly uncorrelated with coverage ratios. Keeping the leg pure rather than blending it with coverage makes the test diagnostic: if it works, maturity structure is a new conditioning dimension for the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: LowDepreciationLevelVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the effect is driven by firms that simply charge little depreciation relative to assets — asset-light or fully depreciated firms with weak debt coverage — then the level, not the within-firm deviation, should carry the return predictability.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the necessary control for the entire depreciation program: the archive has never tested whether the shortfall measures a *change in policy* or merely a cross-sectional characteristic that the deviation construction partly proxies. A weak result here would confirm the mechanism is genuine within-firm earnings management, while a strong result would mean the interaction should be rebuilt around a simpler and much higher-coverage level variable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( dp, at ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ShortfallVsCoverageAndMaturityWall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc))), RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is truly refinancing-constrained when it both lacks cash earnings to service its debt and must roll a large share of that debt imminently, and it is exactly these firms whose sustained depreciation shortfall represents covenant-motivated earnings management.
input_signals.reasoning: Coverage and maturity share are the two distress legs that each worked independently, they measure serviceability versus timing so their errors should be largely uncorrelated, and both are bounded, smoothly distributed ratios — unlike the net-debt stock blend that sacrificed the FMB slope. This is the most promising consolidation available and should improve both forms of evidence rather than trading them off.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ), ratio( dlc, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SevenYearNormShortfallVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 7)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Because depreciation policy drifts over the multi-year life of an asset base, a seven-year norm should capture even more accumulated deferred expense than a five-year norm, provided enough firms have the required history.
input_signals.reasoning: Extending the window from one year to three to five monotonically improved the slope (−2.98, −3.73, −4.36) with no coverage loss, so the horizon has not yet been shown to saturate and one more step is the cheapest remaining test of the mechanism's timescale. Coverage relative to 0.124 is the decisive diagnostic: if it falls materially the gain would be a survivorship artifact and the five-year specification should stand.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( ratio( dp, at ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 7 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProportionalDepreciationShortfallVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5), RATIO(dp, at)), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A 0.5 percentage-point drop in the depreciation rate is trivial for a capital-intensive utility charging 10% of assets but represents a quarter of the expense for an asset-light firm charging 2%, so the economically comparable measure of stretching is the *proportional* shortfall relative to the firm's own normal rate.
input_signals.reasoning: The absolute deviation mechanically loads the short leg with heavy-asset industries, which is likely why industry-neutralizing the accrual leg was roughly break-even — the sector tilt is a scaling artifact rather than information. Normalizing by the firm's own norm removes the capital-intensity scale without discarding cross-industry information, and should raise the slope and Sharpe together.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ), ratio( dp, at ) ), ma( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: OrdinalDepreciationPositionVsDebtCoverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(dp, at), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What identifies a manipulator is that its current depreciation rate sits at the bottom of its own recent history, regardless of the size of the gap, since the ordinal position is immune to one-off asset sales, acquisitions, and restatements that distort the magnitude.
input_signals.reasoning: The five-year peak benchmark underperformed the mean benchmark on the slope (−2.77 versus −4.36), suggesting extreme-value anchors are noisy; an ordinal position statistic uses the entire history yet remains robust to those same outliers. Comparing it against the mean-deviation leader tells us whether the signal lives in the magnitude of the shortfall or merely in its ordering.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( dp, at ), 5 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( ni, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TripleProductShortfallCoverageMaturity

input_signals.hypothesis: The mispricing is concentrated in the joint tail where all three conditions hold at once — sustained depreciation suppression, weak debt-service capacity, and an imminent maturity wall — so a conjunctive score should isolate a smaller but far more extreme short leg.
input_signals.reasoning: Signal 1 aggregates the two distress channels additively, which lets a firm score highly on distress through one channel alone, whereas the triple product requires both, so the pair jointly identifies whether the interaction is conjunctive or compensatory. If the triple product delivers a larger alpha with a similar t-stat, the tails are where the economics lives and the final generation should concentrate there.

input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose cash earnings have failed to cover contractual debt for several consecutive years are genuinely constrained, whereas a single weak year is often transitory; chronic weak coverage should therefore identify the accounting-manipulation incentive far more precisely.
input_signals.reasoning: The accrual leg is already a multi-year state while the distress leg is a single noisy annual flow, an asymmetry that plausibly caps the interaction's precision; smoothing coverage over three years matches the two legs' information horizons. This is the highest-value untested refinement because it improves the conditioning variable's signal-to-noise without adding a new economic dimension, which generation 7 showed to be counterproductive.

input_signals.hypothesis: Debt-service capacity and the sheer size of the contractual debt burden are distinct constraints, and combining them should identify constrained firms better than either alone, provided the stock measure is not distorted by cash netting.
input_signals.reasoning: The net-debt version delivered the archive's largest alpha (−5.3%) but collapsed the slope, most likely because subtracting cash creates a heavily skewed, cash-rich-firm-driven tail; gross interest-bearing debt over assets is bounded, smoothly distributed, and captures the same burden concept. This is a targeted repair of a known failure mode rather than a new blend.

input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(dp, at), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(ni, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset-life stretching is a directional policy that shows up as a steadily declining depreciation rate, so the fitted slope of dp/at over five years measures the manipulation more faithfully than the gap between the latest value and a backward-looking average.
input_signals.reasoning: A deviation from a moving average is contaminated by the manipulated years inside the benchmark itself, mechanically shrinking the measured shortfall for firms that have been suppressing depreciation for years, whereas a trend coefficient accumulates rather than averages away that behavior. This is a different statistic of the same economic state and the generation-1 trend failure is not informative here because that signal extrapolated a *distress* trend, not an accounting-policy trend.

input_signals.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is the accumulated stock of expense that has not yet been recognized, so summing three years of annual shortfalls measures the size of the impending write-down rather than this year's increment.
input_signals.reasoning: If the mechanism is deferral of a real charge, the reversal magnitude should scale with the cumulative deferral, which implies a stock construction should dominate a flow construction on portfolio alpha. Coverage is the key diagnostic since the nested windows require roughly seven years of data, and a large drop would indicate the apparent gain is a survivorship artifact.

input_signals.hypothesis: Two independent symptoms of under-depreciation — a rate below the firm's own norm and an operating asset base growing faster than the depreciation charge — should corroborate each other, so firms exhibiting both are the most likely genuine manipulators.
input_signals.reasoning: Both accrual legs worked with this distress leg (FMB −4.36 and −2.06) and they use different information, since one is a within-firm rate comparison and the other a cross-item growth mismatch, so rank-summing should reduce classification error on the accrual dimension where the archive has only ever combined a depreciation leg with a working-capital leg. input_signals.reasoning: The seven-year norm produced the archive's strongest slope among accrual constructions and chronic coverage produced the strongest overall result on the distress side, and the two changes act on different legs so they should compound rather than conflict. input_signals.reasoning: The trend construction generated the most statistically reliable FF5 alpha in the archive (t = −4.55) when paired with single-year coverage, so upgrading its distress leg to the chronic version that improved every other signal is the natural completion of that experiment. input_signals.reasoning: Moving coverage from one year to a three-year average improved every statistic, so the persistence horizon of the distress leg is an open and unexhausted design parameter, exactly parallel to the norm-window question that produced the largest gains earlier. input_signals.reasoning: Level deviation carries the strongest slope while the trend carries the strongest alpha t-stat, which implies they contain partly distinct information about the same policy state rather than being redundant transformations.
